name: Photomosaic
basis: tiles cropped from the picture, matched by colour descriptors (how)
note: Shares the mosaic idea but models nearest-neighbour matching, not setting.

lumenary.blurb: The picture rebuilt from hundreds of small pieces of itself. Every tile is a crop of the same photograph, picked because its colours fit the spot it has to fill; seen from a step back the pieces melt into the whole.

facts.bestOn: Pictures with a variety of colours; faces and landscapes

why: Seen from far away the picture is one thing; seen up close it is made of hundreds of others. The eye blends whatever is smaller than it can resolve, so a tile needs only the right average colour to disappear into the whole, while keeping enough detail of its own to reward a closer look. Here the tiles are pieces of the same photograph, so the picture is built out of itself.
how: Cut the picture into pieces at four sizes, and add a mirrored copy of each.
Describe every piece by the average colour of its four quarters and of the whole.
Describe every cell of the grid in the same way, from the picture itself.
Pick for each cell the piece with the nearest description, with a growing penalty for pieces already used, and never the same as a neighbour.
Shift the tile’s colours towards what the cell needs, a little less in the darkest and lightest cells, and lay it down with a small gap.
history: Mosaics of small stones, called tesserae, are thousands of years old, and the Romans and Byzantines used tiny coloured pieces to make pictures that read from across a hall. The photographic version came in the 1990s: in 1993 Robert Silvers, then at MIT, developed software that built a picture from many small photographs, and mosaic posters made of family snapshots were familiar by the end of the decade. The matching step is a nearest-neighbour search, now used all over computing.
uses: Memory collages from a photo album
Large prints seen from far and near
terms: One small piece of stone, glass or tile in a mosaic.
The item in a collection whose description is closest to a given one.
The short list of numbers, here average colours, that stands for a tile when matching.
paragraphs: Each tile and each cell of the grid is described by a signature of 15 numbers: the mean red, green and blue of its four quarters, and of the whole. The library holds square crops at four sizes, 0.11, 0.17, 0.26 and 0.4 of the picture’s short side, at positions on a jittered grid, together with a mirrored copy of each. For a cell, the cost of tile t is D(t) = the sum of (s_cell - s_t)^2 over the first 12 numbers (the four quarters) + 0.35 lambda u_t, where u_t is the number of times t has been used and lambda rises from 1 to 1401 with the variety slider. The cheapest tile wins, except that it can never be the tile to the left or the one above.

The tile is then fitted to its cell. Its pixels v are moved towards the cell’s mean colour m_c: v' = (1 - k) v + k (m_c + delta (v - m_t)), where m_t is the tile’s own mean, k is the colour match slider, and delta = 0.38 + 0.62 (1 - |l - 128| / 128) keeps less detail in very dark and very light cells, where a real print would have little contrast. At k = 1 every tile has exactly the average colour of its cell, and detail is all that remains of the original tile. The gap, up to 10% of a cell on each side, shows the grout.

equations.note: The cost of using tile t in a cell: u_t is how often it is already used and V is the variety slider (0 to 1).
Colour fitting: v is a tile pixel, m_t the tile’s mean, m_c the cell’s mean and k the colour match.
How much of the tile’s own detail is kept, by the brightness l of the cell.

presets.text: More tiles with a thin gap give the effect of a screen.
Tiles that each show the whole picture make a classic mosaic of copies.
A low colour match keeps the tiles’ own colours and shows more of each small picture.
